short: The last Jewish rebel stronghold fell after a Roman siege ramp ended a mass suicide standoff.
full:
Masada, Herod the Great's clifftop fortress above the Dead Sea, became the refuge of the Sicarii rebel faction after Jerusalem's fall in 70 CE. The Roman governor Lucius Flavius Silva besieged it with the Tenth Legion and thousands of auxiliaries and Jewish prisoners, who built a massive earthen ramp up the fortress's western slope, an engineering effort still visible today.

When Roman troops breached the walls around 73 or 74 CE, they found most of the roughly 960 defenders dead, having reportedly chosen suicide over capture and enslavement, according to the sole surviving account by Josephus, who was not present. Modern scholars debate how literally to take his narrative. The siege closed the First Jewish-Roman War and, revived as a national symbol in twentieth-century Israel, became one of ancient history's most contested episodes of resistance and memory.
